title: Calculus Investigation Starter
subject: Calculus
summary: A clarity-first scaffold for investigating functions, derivatives, critical points, convexity, and definite integrals with exact bounded examples.
details: This starter helps an instructor build a calculus Class around rational-coefficient polynomials on bounded rational intervals. It supplies explicit language, notation, examples, nonexamples, and a deterministic investigation palette while leaving course identity, sequencing, Study binding, and publication policy to the instructor.

objectives: Connect the formal difference quotient to the slope of a polynomial at a point.
Use derivative information to identify critical points and reason about shape.
Form and test bounded claims relating degree, critical points, convexity, and integrals.
Treat a counterexample as evidence for revising hypotheses rather than as a failed activity.

concepts.title: Function on a closed interval
concepts.plain_language: A function assigns exactly one output to every allowed input in an interval that includes both endpoints.
concepts.formal_definition: For real numbers a ≤ b, a function on [a,b] is a map f:[a,b]→ℝ such that each x∈[a,b] has one value f(x)∈ℝ.

notation.meaning: the set of real x satisfying a ≤ x ≤ b
the unique output assigned to input x

steps: Check that each x in [-1,2] has one squared value.
Evaluate the endpoints: f(-1)=1 and f(2)=4.
worked_example.conclusion: The rule defines a function f:[-1,2]→ℝ.

nonexample.explanation: For x>0 it permits both y=√x and y=-√x, so it does not assign exactly one output unless a branch is chosen.

concepts.title: Derivative at a point
concepts.plain_language: The derivative records the instantaneous rate at which a function changes near one input.
concepts.formal_definition: For an interior point c of the domain, f′(c)=lim_{h→0}(f(c+h)-f(c))/h when this finite limit exists.

notation.meaning: the derivative of f at c
h approaches zero through nonzero values

worked_example.prompt: Find the derivative of f(x)=x² at c=3.
steps: Expand and simplify to 6+h for h≠0.
Take the limit as h approaches 0.

nonexample.prompt: Claim that f(x)=|x| has derivative 0 at x=0 because f(0)=0.
nonexample.explanation: A function value is not a derivative. The right difference quotients approach 1 and the left ones approach -1, so the derivative does not exist.

concepts.title: Differentiable on an interval
concepts.plain_language: A function is differentiable on an interval when it has a derivative at every interior point, with appropriate one-sided derivatives at included endpoints.
concepts.formal_definition: A function f:[a,b]→ℝ is differentiable on [a,b] when f′(x) exists for every x∈(a,b), the right derivative exists at a, and the left derivative exists at b.

notation.meaning: the derivative function where it exists

worked_example.prompt: Decide whether f(x)=x³ is differentiable on [-2,2].
steps: It converges to 3x² at every interior point and has the corresponding one-sided endpoint limits.

nonexample.explanation: The one-sided slopes disagree at the interior point 0, so the function is not differentiable on the whole interval.

concepts.title: Convex on an interval
concepts.plain_language: A function is convex when every chord between two points on its graph stays on or above the graph.
concepts.formal_definition: A function f on an interval I is convex when f(tx+(1-t)y) ≤ t f(x)+(1-t) f(y) for all x,y∈I and t∈[0,1].

notation.meaning: a point between x and y

worked_example.prompt: Explain why f(x)=x² is convex on ℝ.
steps: The difference is t(1-t)(x-y)², which is nonnegative for t∈[0,1].
worked_example.conclusion: Therefore (tx+(1-t)y)²≤t x²+(1-t)y², exactly the convexity inequality.

nonexample.explanation: The midpoint value 0 is greater than the average of the endpoint values -1, violating the convexity inequality.

concepts.title: Polynomial degree
concepts.plain_language: The degree is the largest exponent whose coefficient is not zero.
concepts.formal_definition: For p(x)=a₀+a₁x+⋯+aₙxⁿ with aₙ≠0, degree(p)=n. The zero polynomial requires a separate convention and is excluded from this starter palette.

notation.meaning: the largest exponent with nonzero coefficient

steps: List exponents with nonzero coefficients: 3, 1, and 0.

nonexample.explanation: The coefficient 5 is not an exponent. The largest nonzero exponent is 2.

concepts.title: Interior critical-point count
concepts.plain_language: This count records how many interior inputs have derivative zero or no derivative.
concepts.formal_definition: For f on [a,b], a critical point is c∈(a,b) where f′(c)=0 or f′(c) does not exist. The invariant is the number of distinct such c in the bounded object representation.

notation.meaning: the tangent slope at c is zero

worked_example.prompt: Count the critical points of f(x)=x³-3x on [-2,2].
steps: Solve 3x²-3=0 to get x=-1 and x=1.
Both solutions lie in the interior.

nonexample.prompt: Count both endpoints of f(x)=x on [0,1] as critical points.
nonexample.explanation: This starter's definition counts interior points only; endpoints are excluded and the derivative is never zero inside.

concepts.title: Definite integral
concepts.plain_language: The definite integral is the signed accumulation of function values across an interval.
concepts.formal_definition: For an integrable f:[a,b]→ℝ, ∫ₐᵇf(x)dx is the limit of Riemann sums Σ f(ξᵢ)Δxᵢ as the largest subinterval width approaches zero.

nonexample.prompt: Claim ∫₋₁¹ x dx=1 because the triangular area has size 1.
nonexample.explanation: The integral is signed: the negative and positive triangular contributions cancel, so the value is 0.

object_family.label: Rational-coefficient polynomials on bounded rational intervals
object_family.scope: Nonzero polynomials of degree at most 8 with bounded rational coefficients, paired with a closed rational interval.
object_family.representation: coefficient vector and ordered interval endpoints

invariants.label: Definite integral over the selected interval
